title: VAT on UAE property: residential, commercial, and off-plan cases people get wrong
summary: Learn how VAT applies to residential, commercial and off-plan property in the UAE, along with the critical information on where people go wrong
body_markdown:
If you are based in the UAE, it's common knowledge that VAT on most items and their transactions is a standard 5%, and in certain situations, 0%, and in others, entirely exempt. The same holds for real estate transactions as well, be it a sale or a lease.


That said, if you do deal with the finances of these transactions, you must know VAT is applied differently depending on whether the property in question is commercial, residential, bare land, or a mixed-use development.


How VAT is treated also changes depending on whether the property is being sold for the first time or is a subsequent sale. While all of this information is available on the FTA's official Real Estate VAT Guide, it's a very lengthy document to go through, especially when you are trying to streamline[spend management for real estate groups](https://www.alaan.com/industries/real-estate) .


This guide gives you a snapshot of all the critical information you need to identify the correct VAT treatment for each scenario, determine if input VAT can be recovered in that scenario, and walk through the specific cases you're most likely to get wrong and when it's worthwhile to get professional advice.


## A snapshot of the various VAT treatment scenarios in the UAE


Every real estate supply you make in the UAE falls into one of three categories: standard-rated at 5%, zero-rated at 0%, or exempt.


VAT Treatment Rate Applies to Can input VAT be recovered?


Standard-rated 5% Commercial property sales, commercial leases, hotels, developed commercial land Yes, subject to normal VAT rules


Zero-rated 0% First supply of a new residential building within three years of completion, certain charitable buildings Yes


Exempt No VAT Charged Residential leases, subsequent sales of residential property, bare land Generally no, where costs relate to exempt supplies


It's critical to understand these distinctions because two transactions can involve similar properties while attracting completely different VAT treatments. Also, zero-rated supplies let you recover input VAT on related costs in full, while exempt supplies generally don't.


If you need a refresher on calculating VAT amounts after identifying the correct treatment, Alaan's guide on[calculating VAT in the UAE](https://www.alaan.com/blog/calculate-vat-uae) covers the calculations.


## VAT on residential property in the UAE


VAT on residential properties in the UAE requires careful attention, as two different VAT treatments can apply depending on the transaction in question.


In general, the lease of residential property is exempt from VAT. The same applies to the sale of an existing residential property after its first supply. The term "first supply" is the official legal term that refers to the first sale or lease of a property within three years of the building's date of completion.


According to[Section 3.2 of VATGRE1](https://tax.gov.ae/DownloadOpenTextFile?fileUrl=en%2FVAT_VAT_Guides%2FReal_Estate_Guide%2FReal_Estate_Guide_VATGRE1_EN_19_04_2021_EN.pdf) , the first supply of a new residential building made within three years of its completion is zero-rated. Any subsequent sales generally become exempt.


Type of Transaction VAT Treatment Input VAT Recovery Key Conditions


First Supply Zero-rated (0%) Recoverable in full Must occur within 3 years of the completion date.
Includes the very first sale or lease.
Subsequent sales within the 3-year window do not qualify.


Subsequent Sales / General Leases Exempt Generally not recoverable Applies to any sale or lease after the "first supply" has already taken place.
Also applies to any subsequent sales that fall within the initial 3-year window if made by someone other than the original developer/first supplier.

## VAT on commercial property in the UAE


VAT on commercial property in the UAE is a straightforward affair, as it's subject to VAT at the standard rate of 5% regardless if its being sold or leased. If the property is being rented, the landlord will charge 5% VAT on rent as well.


As a tenant, if they are VAT registered and are using the premises for taxable business activities, this VAT may normally be recoverable as input tax. For the landlords, this rental income also counts towards the VAT registration threshold.


If taxable supplies exceed the mandatory registration threshold, VAT registration becomes compulsory under the normal UAE VAT rules.


The one caveat is if you are operating in a free zone, you also need to consider whether any additional VAT rules apply to it. Alaan's guide to[VAT for free zone companies](https://www.alaan.com/blog/vat-for-free-zone-companies-in-uae) covers these nuances in detail.


Type of Transaction VAT Treatment Input VAT Recovery Key Conditions


Sale of Commercial Property Standard rate (5%) N/A Applies regardless of whether the property is being sold or leased.


Lease / Rental of Commercial Property Standard rate (5%) Recoverable for VAT-registered tenants using the premises for taxable business activities, and counts towards the registration threshold for landlords. Landlords must charge 5% VAT on rent.
Compulsory VAT registration applies if taxable supplies exceed the mandatory threshold.


Free Zone Operations Varies N/A Requires consideration of additional/special VAT rules that may apply to free zones.


The FTA's own registration guidance at[tax.gov.ae](https://tax.gov.ae/) sets out the thresholds that apply once your taxable supplies, commercial rent included, cross the mandatory or voluntary registration limits.


## Bare land and developed land


Another area that is a frequent source of confusion in the context of VAT is land. This confusion can be avoided by simply understanding the difference between what bare and developed land is.


### Bare Land


Bare land, as the name alludes to, is land that has no completed buildings, partially completed buildings or civil engineering works on it. It is exempt from VAT.


Fences, temporary structures and buildings that have not been built beyond the foundation do not change a plot from bare to developed land.


### Developed Land


Any land is considered developed once it's "covered," per Section 6 of VATGRE1. Covered here can refer to completed buildings, infrastructure, or civil engineering works that are above ground.


If a building is built beyond its foundation or if there are civil works like a pipeline that break the surface to allow a future connection, the land is considered covered and will be subject to the standard VAT rate depending on the nature of the property.


### Mixed-use buildings


If you own a mixed-use development, i.e., with buildings with clearly distinct areas carrying different VAT treatments, you need to apportion it.


The commercial floors are taxed at 5%, the residential floors follow the standard exempt or zero-rated residential rules, and you split the value accordingly if you sell the building as a whole.


Here, per Section 7 of VATGRE1, you can:


- Recover VAT in full on costs directly attributable to taxable commercial supplies.
- Exclude VAT directly attributable to exempt residential supplies.
- Apportion shared costs using a fair and reasonable method accepted under the VAT legislation.


## Recovering input VAT on property costs


Whether you can recover input VAT depends less on what you bought and more on what the purchase relates to. Per the FTA's Real Estate VAT Guide, as a business you can generally recover input VAT on costs that relate to taxable supplies, but not on costs that relate to exempt supplies.


Here is how that applies in the real world:


The activity Is VAT recoverable Why?


First supply of a new residential building (zero-rated) Yes Zero-rated supplies are still taxable supplies, so related input VAT is generally recoverable.


Leasing or selling existing residential property (exempt) Usually no Input VAT directly attributable to exempt supplies is generally not recoverable.


Developing or selling commercial property Yes Commercial supplies are standard-rated taxable supplies.


Mixed-use developments Partially Input VAT must be apportioned between taxable and exempt activities using an FTA-accepted method.


It is vital to understand the distinctions between each instance.


Once your residential building's first supply has happened, any further costs you incur, agent fees on a later lease, ongoing maintenance, general upkeep, relate to what is now an exempt supply. You can't reclaim VAT on those costs, even though you fully recovered the original construction VAT.


Another scennario is when you are transacting with other VAT-registered entities. in this case, your recovery eligibility also depends partly on the counterparty's own VAT position.[Alaan's guide to B2B VAT rules in the UAE](https://www.alaan.com/blog/b2b-vat-rules-uae-guide) covers this in detail.


Getting input recovery right also has a direct effect on cash flow, particularly if you're carrying large construction costs ahead of a zero-rated first supply, something[Alaan's guide on VAT in the UAE for cash flow](https://www.alaan.com/blog/advantages-disadvantages-vat-uae-businesses) explores further.


And if you're managing staff who front costs on your company's behalf, the same recoverability logic applies to[VAT on expense reimbursement](https://www.alaan.com/blog/employee-expense-reimbursement-taxable-implications) : what the expense relates to determines what's recoverable, not who paid for it first.


## Five property VAT situations people often get wrong


Some of the most expensive VAT mistakes come from applying the right rule to the wrong type of property. Here are the five scenarios that most often top that list.


The Assumption The right approach to the situation


Every residential property sale is VAT exempt The first supply of a qualifying new residential building within three years is generally zero-rated. Later sales are generally exempt.


VAT never applies to land sales This applies only to bare land. Developed commercial land is generally standard-rated.


Residential rent always includes VAT. Residential leasing is generally exempt from VAT, while commercial leasing is generally standard-rated.


Developers cannot recover VAT on residential projects VAT relating to qualifying first supplies of new residential buildings is generally recoverable because those supplies are zero-rated.


One VAT treatment applies to the entire mixed-use building. Commercial and residential portions may require different VAT treatments, with shared costs apportioned appropriately.


## Summing it up


The key to getting VAT on property in the UAE right is to focus on identifying **** what kind of property transaction you're dealing with. That will determine if the transaction is VAT exempt, zero-rated, or standard-rated and affects everything from the VAT you charge to whether you can recover VAT on construction, maintenance, and operating costs.


That said, getting the treatment right on paper is only half the job. ## FAQs


**What is the VAT rate on commercial property rent in the UAE?**


Commercial property leases are generally subject to VAT at the standard rate of 5%, provided the landlord is VAT registered or required to register.


**Does VAT apply to the sale of land in the UAE?**


Bare land is generally exempt from VAT, while developed commercial land is generally subject to VAT at the standard rate.


**Who is exempt from VAT on UAE property?**


If you own or lease existing residential property, or sell or lease bare land, you make exempt supplies. The first supply of a new residential building is zero-rated rather than exempt, a distinction that matters for your input VAT recovery.


**Can VAT paid on purchasing commercial property be recovered?**


If the commercial property is acquired for making taxable business supplies and the normal VAT recovery conditions are met, businesses may generally recover the input VAT incurred.


**Is there property tax in the UAE?**


The UAE does not levy an annual property tax similar to many other countries. However, buyers, sellers, landlords, and tenants may still pay municipality fees, registration fees, or other government charges depending on the emirate and the transaction.
